newsitem.title: UK: European debt futures enjoy relief as Fed sticks.
newsitem.headline: European debt futures enjoy relief as Fed sticks.

text.p: European debt futures breathed a sigh of relief on Wednesday as the prospect of higher interest rates in the U.S. was pushed down the line, analysts said.

While German Bund futures led the way with a 23 basis point jump higher at the open, French and Italian debt futures powered through to set new contract highs. "There is a bit of relief out there," said Jonathan York, a futures broker at Cater Allen on London's LIFFE floor.
"There is a good atmosphere and things are looking quite nice for now," he said.

Analysts said the respite for U.S. debt -- which gained on Tuesday after the Federal Reserve decided to keep U.S. monetary policy on hold -- may be shortlived, but they said European bonds may be able to bask a little longer.

"The fact that they haven't raised rates in the U.S. is slightly inflationary at the long-end, said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London. "Once the initial euphoria has gone, the U.S. (market) will come down."
After a strong opening, German Bund futures held their ground in early trade. They were trading 22 basis points higher at 98.39 by 0719 GMT.

French December notionnel futures set a new contract high at 124.40, crashing through the previous 124.26 record with the first trade of the day, while Italy's December BTP contract replaced Tuesday's record high with another at 119.90.
British gilts had a slightly more moderate start as domestic political concerns kept a cap on their gains. December gilt futures were 7/32 higher at 107-22 by 0733 GMT.

Players said positive sentiment was evident on the LIFFE trading floor, since many had said before the key U.S. policy-setting meeting on Tuesday that any move on interest rates would be a very close call.

The latest poll of views, conducted by Reuters on Tuesday, showed that a slim majority of economists -- 31 of 55 surveyed -- had expected the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to raise the 5.25 percent federal funds rate.

U.S. December T-bond futures gained almost one full point to a high at 109-00 on the news, but later recoiled to close 17/32 higher at 108-20. By 0746 GMT on Wednesday the futures contract was quoted 4/32 down at 108-16 in automated trade.
"If you take away Fed tightening for now and it gives a slightly softer tone to the dollar, European bonds can certainly do well in the short term," said economist Andrew Bevan.
"Really this is another nail in the coffin for talk of higher interest rates in Japan and even of Bundesbank policy starting to turn," said Bevan, Goldman Sach's senior bond economist in London.
But analysts said the outlook for European debt further out and towards the end of this year was less chirpy.
"The U.S. market will come to the conclusion that the Fed is behind the curve," said Bevan. "And when that happens it is going to be difficult for European bonds too."
